findings.title: Findings converge on `listen()`'s parse-and-dispatch of the full `WsServerMessage` union
findings.why_it_matters: D5's ratified contract has `listen` parse every known `WsServerMessage` and dispatch it. Two separate findings hit the same mechanism. Finding 2: the contract has no way to tell "unknown type" (skip) from "known type that failed to parse" (end the stream, per the Posture), because the union is a strict discriminated union. Finding 3: parsing every type makes the whole union, including messages hass-hassette never uses (`execution_completed`, `service_status`, `log_hint`, ...), into client contract, and no compat check covers it. Each finding proposes its own patch: a tag-set export for Finding 2, a compat-check extension for Finding 3. One decision, which types `listen` parses at all, would settle both. Should the parse-and-dispatch scope be re-evaluated (including whether `listen` should parse types the caller doesn't handle, and whether the Posture's "a known type that fails to parse ends the stream" should apply to them) before patching each finding separately?
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate `listen()`'s parse-and-dispatch scope before addressing Findings 2 and 3 individually. Open questions: which message types `listen` parses; how a known type is told apart from an unknown one; which types become client contract and need compat coverage; whether a parse failure of a type the caller never uses should end the stream.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate `listen()`'s parse-and-dispatch scope before addressing Findings 2 and 3 individually.

findings.title: "Skip unknown types" has no mechanism under a strict discriminated union
findings.why_it_matters: D5's contract says `listen` "logs and skips unknown types at debug", and the Posture says "a known type that fails to parse ends the stream". `WsServerMessage` is `Annotated[..., Field(discriminator="type")]`, so validating it against a message with a new `type` raises a validation error. `LenientValue` only covers unknown values of enum or Literal fields, not unknown union tags. An implementation that just validates the union ends hass-hassette's stream on the first new server message type, which is exactly what parent D3 and the `hassette_wire` docstring forbid. The ledger never says how "known" is decided.
findings.recommended: A: In D5's contract, `listen` reads `type` first, checks it against the tags of the union members in the installed `hassette_wire` (derived, not hand-listed), skips unknown types at debug, and validates only known ones, so a validation error means a malformed known type.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Dispatching every known type makes the whole union client contract with no compat coverage
findings.why_it_matters: Today only the frontend consumes the WS schema. After this, hass-hassette's `listen` receives `execution_completed` (high-frequency batches), `log_hint`, `connectivity`, `service_status` and `apps_changed`, none of which it needs. Under the Posture, a parse failure of any of them raises out of `listen`. The WS compat check compares the schema's shape. The client compat check (`nox -s client_compat`) replays HTTP fixtures only and has no WS path, so nothing tests the released client's parsing against HEAD's WS messages. And the outage isn't one reconnect long: every reconnect dies at the next message of the failing type, so push stays dead until a client release (the poll keeps correctness).
findings.recommended: A: `listen` parses and dispatches only caller-requested types and skips the rest unvalidated.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A publish failure after the commit makes `set()` raise for a value that is already committed
findings.why_it_matters: `set_job` commits the row (`persist_state`), updates memory and bumps `revision`. D2 adds the publish after that. Any exception from the publish propagates out of `run_write`, so the app's `set()` raises even though the value is durably committed and already visible in the listing. Possible sources: building the `DeclaredEntity`, `broadcast`'s `json.dumps(default=str)` round-trip, and `service_not_wired_error` from the `runtime_query_service` accessor. The last is concrete: `_runtime_query_service` is set only in `Hassette.wire_services()`, and the test harness never calls it, so a publish that goes through the accessor makes every harness test of `set()` raise. The design's Assumed section says the publish "must work, or find no clients, in a harness `Hassette`" but doesn't say how. The Posture's "loud failure" and parent D6 were written about a failed write, not a failed notification after a successful one.
findings.recommended: A: State in D2 that the publish can't fail for expected reasons: it builds from the wire model, finds no clients when `RuntimeQueryService` isn't wired (harness), and does not use the raising accessor. A remaining exception is a bug and propagates.
findings.chosen: A: State in D2 that the publish can't fail for expected reasons: it builds from the wire model, finds no clients when `RuntimeQueryService` isn't wired (harness), and does not use the raising accessor. A remaining exception is a bug and propagates.
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether the app-testing harness should wire RuntimeQueryService; kept it out after the explanation

findings.title: `HassetteConnectionError` describes an HTTP-request failure, and handshake rejection is unmapped
findings.why_it_matters: `HassetteConnectionError`'s docstring says "The request never got a complete HTTP response". `listen` will raise it for post-handshake ends (server close on every hassette restart, heartbeat timeout, mid-stream reset), which that docstring doesn't describe. A bad token is rejected before `accept()` with `websocket.close(...)`, which reaches the client as an HTTP 403 handshake rejection with no problem body. Over REST a bad token is a 401 `AuthenticationError`, but `error_class_for(403, None)` gives `ForbiddenError`. The ledger says only "`HassetteConnectionError` (or the matching existing subclass)". So the same bad token surfaces as different classes on REST and `/ws`, or aiohttp's `WSServerHandshakeError` leaks, which would break the module's "never a raw aiohttp exception" promise.
findings.recommended: A: Map handshake rejection through `error_class_for(status, None)`, widen `HassetteConnectionError`'s docstring to cover stream ends, and document that a bad token on `/ws` surfaces as `ForbiddenError`.
findings.chosen: Fix server: 401 problem denial
findings.choice_reason: User sensed a server-side smell; chose fixing /ws to reject with REST's 401 problem and count failed auth

findings.title: D2's revision-order guarantee relies on the publish being built and awaited inline, which the ledger doesn't say
findings.why_it_matters: `broadcast` is `async` and awaits `self._lock`, so it yields between `revision += 1` and the queue puts. Today the single writer is blocked on this job, so nothing reorders. But D2's whole argument for option A is this order, and it holds only while the publish is awaited inline and takes the already-built values rather than re-reading state after an await. A later refactor to a fire-and-forget publish (`create_task`) would silently reorder deltas, and the poll would hide it.
findings.chosen: Add to D2's contract (the Ratified sentence's follow-on, or a line under it): the publish method takes the already-built `boot_id`, `revision`, instance key and entity as arguments, is awaited inline in `set_job` right after the bump (never spawned as a task), and reads no service state after its first await. Add to the Build step a test that two back-to-back `set()` calls reach a registered client queue in revision order.

findings.title: D1 doesn't fix the message's envelope or class names
findings.why_it_matters: D1 says the message becomes wire contract once #73 depends on it, but its field list is flat (`boot_id`, `revision`, `app_key`, `instance_name`, `entity`) and doesn't say whether these sit inside `data` like every other `/ws` message (`{type, data, timestamp}`) or at the top level. The class names aren't given either. Left open, the shape gets chosen implicitly at build time and then freezes.
findings.chosen: Add one line to D1: the message follows the existing envelope, `EntityStateChangedWsMessage` with `type: "entity_state_changed"`, `data: EntityStateChangedData` and `timestamp`, and `EntityStateChangedData` carries `boot_id`, `revision`, `app_key`, `instance_name` and `entity: DeclaredEntity` (names per the `hassette_wire` naming rule).

findings.title: The client docs must state what `revision` does and doesn't guarantee
findings.why_it_matters: `revision` is hassette-wide and is bumped by `commit_job` with no `/ws` message (D4) as well as by `set_job`. A receiver can't tell a missed delta from a declaration commit, so a gap in revisions proves nothing, and the apply rule compares a hassette-wide number per instance. Parent D3 already settles this ("counters may skip values"; the poll repairs loss). But the ledger's only planned consumer-facing statement is a python-client docs section, and the design doesn't say that section carries these rules. Without it, a reader of the published contract could treat revision as gap evidence.
findings.chosen: Extend the Summary's "Docs" bullet: the python-client streaming section states that `revision` orders entity messages and listings within one `boot_id`; that it isn't contiguous (declaration commits bump it with no message, D4), so a gap proves nothing; and that a lost delta is repaired only by the next listing (the poll, or the refetch on reconnect). Cite parent D3 and spec 158 D4 as the source.

findings.title: A dropped delta is invisible to the client
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a single user with a handful of apps; at the stated scale a documented limit is enough. `listen` awaits `on_connected` (listing fetch plus entity creation) before reading, so deltas pile up in the 256-slot queue during the resync window, which they share with UI traffic such as `execution_completed`. An overflow is counted and logged only on the server. Because `revision` is global and not contiguous (Finding 8), the client can't detect the gap. D1's ratification already accepts "a dropped delta stays stale until the next poll". The new point is that the client gets no signal and can't resync early.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a delta dropped from a full client queue is invisible to the client and stays stale until the next 30 s poll.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a delta dropped from a full client queue is invisible to the client and stays stale until the next 30 s poll.
findings.choice_reason: Noted #4217 (close slow clients) is the real fix

findings.title: A delta from an older boot can be applied over a fresher listing, and `connected` carries no `boot_id`
findings.why_it_matters: The senior engineer's main scenario (a new-boot delta discarded as numerically older) is already covered by inherited rules: parent D3 has the integration drop its last-applied marks when the boot identifier changes, and spec 158 D4 says to compare `boot_id` before `revision`. The remaining gap is the reverse direction. If hassette restarts after `connected` but before `on_connected` fetches the listing, the listing comes from the new boot while deltas already queued on the old socket carry the old boot. A boot id has no order, so "drop marks when the boot changes" would apply the old-boot delta over the fresh listing, until the old socket closes and the reconnect refetches. The `connected` message carries no `boot_id`, so the client can't tell which boot the socket belongs to.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hassette restart between `connected` and the listing fetch can let old-boot deltas overwrite the fresh listing until the old socket closes and the reconnect refetches.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hassette restart between `connected` and the listing fetch can let old-boot deltas overwrite the fresh listing until the old socket closes and the reconnect refetches.
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether peers put a boot id in their connect message; none do

findings.title: On the `aiohttp>=3.10` floor, a callback blocking about 45 s closes a healthy stream
findings.why_it_matters: The critic flagged this as unverified. It is now verified. In aiohttp 3.10.0, the heartbeat and pong timers are reset only when `receive()` returns a frame: `_reset_heartbeat` runs after `self._reader.read()`, and `_cancel_heartbeat` cancels the pong timer. So while `listen` is blocked in `on_connected` or `on_message`, a pong that arrives can't cancel the pong deadline. With D6's 30 s heartbeat, a callback that blocks for about 45 s (30 s plus the 15 s pong wait) closes a healthy socket with a timeout. The installed aiohttp 3.14.5 resets on data received at the reader (`_on_data_received`), so it doesn't have this behavior.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: on aiohttp releases before reader-side heartbeat reset, a `listen` callback that blocks for about 45 s ends a healthy stream, and the caller's reconnect handles it.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: on aiohttp releases before reader-side heartbeat reset, a `listen` callback that blocks for about 45 s ends a healthy stream, and the caller's reconnect handles it.

findings.title: Subscribe-before-fetch depends on the caller putting its listing fetch in `on_connected`
findings.why_it_matters: D5's ratified shape puts the ordering burden on the caller, and the ledger accepts that. Nothing in `listen` enforces it. Fetching the listing before calling `listen`, or outside `on_connected`, works in every test and loses deltas only under load. The critic doesn't ask to reopen D5. It asks only that the docs show the correct pattern, so the ratified trade-off doesn't become a trap.
findings.recommended: A: Keep D5, and have the python-client docs show the listing fetch inside `on_connected`, with the reason.
findings.chosen: One sentence in the docstring
findings.choice_reason: Questioned whether docs were needed; chose a one-sentence docstring over a docs example

findings.title: An old client on a newer server silently never gets push
`listen`'s docstring doesn't say an older server's bad-token rejection raises `ForbiddenError`
findings.why_it_matters: D9's contract is "a bad token raises `AuthenticationError` from `listen` exactly as from REST", but that comes from the server change. A hassette server released before this change still closes the handshake with a bodyless 403, which `handshake_error` maps through `error_class_for(403)` to `ForbiddenError`. hass-hassette's reauth keys on `AuthenticationError` (D9's stated reason), so against an older server a rotated token gives a "forbidden" error instead of a reauth prompt. The docs page states this, but the `listen` docstring, which is what a caller reads at the call site, lists only `AuthenticationError`. The project rule is that user-facing methods carry their full docstrings.
findings.chosen: In `HassetteClient.listen`'s Raises block, after the `AuthenticationError` entry, add: `ForbiddenError: A hassette server older than the release that added ``listen`` rejected the token with a bare 403 instead of a 401; treat it as a rejected token.` No code change. The heavier alternative the critic named (bumping `API_SCHEMA_VERSION`/`MIN_API_SCHEMA_VERSION` so `check_server_version` rejects such servers) contradicts the ratified Rollout stance and the docs page, so it isn't applied.

findings.title: The 401 denial depends on the `websockets-sansio` backend, but nothing at the line that picks the backend says so
findings.why_it_matters: `websocket_endpoint` calls `send_denial_response` unconditionally. Starlette raises `RuntimeError` on a server without the ASGI WebSocket Denial Response extension, and before uvicorn 0.52.1 the `websockets-sansio` backend sent an invalid HTTP response for it. The constraint is written in the route docstring (`ws.py`) and the Build notes, but the code that can break it is `ws="websockets-sansio"` in `web_api_service.py`, which has no comment. The live 401 test doesn't protect that line: it starts its own uvicorn with `ws="websockets-sansio"` hard-coded, so switching the production backend (to wsproto, say) leaves the test green and turns every bad-token handshake into a server error. This is a rule living apart from the code it protects, so it costs something on every read of that config, not only when it breaks.
findings.recommended: A: Add a comment next to `ws="websockets-sansio"` in `web_api_service.py` saying the `/ws` 401 denial (`send_denial_response`) needs this backend's denial-response support, fixed in uvicorn 0.52.1 (the `pyproject.toml` floor).
findings.chosen: A: Add a comment next to `ws="websockets-sansio"` in `web_api_service.py` saying the `/ws` 401 denial (`send_denial_response`) needs this backend's denial-response support, fixed in uvicorn 0.52.1 (the `pyproject.toml` floor).

findings.title: The failed-auth tracker docstring says a source failing on both paths is "counted once", but a browser's rejected reconnect is counted twice
findings.why_it_matters: D9 adds `/ws` handshake failures to the tracker. When a browser tab's socket closes before opening, the web UI calls `confirmAuthRejection()`, which makes a REST request that also 401s and is also recorded. So every reconnect attempt from a tab with an expired session adds two entries for one source. The tracker only emits a coalesced WARN at `FAILED_AUTH_THRESHOLD` (10 in 5 minutes) and is documented as a logging aid, not a control, so the effect is a WARN that fires in half as many cycles and overstates how many credentials were tried. The new `failed_auth_tracker()` docstring says "a source failing on both is counted once", which reads as per-attempt deduplication. The code does the opposite: both paths record into one shared tally. That docstring is wrong on every read, whether or not anyone sees the WARN.
findings.recommended: A: Reword the `failed_auth_tracker` docstring to say the HTTP gate and the `/ws` handshake feed one tally, so a browser's rejected reconnect (the handshake plus the web UI's confirming REST call) counts twice.
findings.chosen: A: Reword the `failed_auth_tracker` docstring to say the HTTP gate and the `/ws` handshake feed one tally, so a browser's rejected reconnect (the handshake plus the web UI's confirming REST call) counts twice.

findings.title: Entity traffic shares the UI's bounded queues and their single drop counter
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: apps that set sensors at a steady high rate (tens of messages per second), a deployment the corpus's 25-sensor app approaches. Every `/ws` client has one 256-slot queue. Under D3, entity messages go to every client, so a chatty app's sets can fill a backgrounded UI tab's queue and push out the messages the UI does use (`app_status_changed`, `service_status`, `connectivity`, `execution_completed`). The overflow bumps `WS_BROADCAST_CLIENT_QUEUE_FULL` and logs "Dropped N messages". That counter and WARN don't say which type was dropped, so a lost entity delta (HA stale for up to 30 s) can't be told from a lost `execution_completed` batch. The browser also runs the generated validator over every entity message before discarding it. The ledger already priced the queue sharing ("Queue pressure on UI tabs: Entity messages share the UI's 256 slots", D3) and accepted that a dropped delta is undetectable (D1). Neither critic argues the stance is wrong; data-integrity says "probably leave it until #4217".
findings.recommended: B: Keep D1/D3 as ratified; #4217 and #4418 own the fix.
findings.chosen: B: Keep D1/D3 as ratified; #4217 and #4418 own the fix.

findings.title: A publish failure after the commit makes `set()` raise for a write that landed, and a retry republishes nothing
findings.why_it_matters: In `set_job`, the row is committed, memory updated and `revision` bumped before `publish_entity_state` is awaited. An exception from `declared_entity_from`, `EntityStateChangedData` validation or the broadcast reaches the app as a failed `set()` for state that is already durable and visible. A retry with the same value hits the `current.state == state` early return, so nothing republishes and HA waits for the next poll. The service logs nothing itself, so the symptom is "set() raised but the sensor changed anyway". D2 accepted this explicitly ("there is no catch: an exception left is a bug and propagates out of `set()`"). The new points are the no-op retry and the absence of a test that pins the propagation. No critic can name a trigger: `check_value` rejects NaN and non-finite values, `check_attributes` round-trips attributes through `json.dumps(allow_nan=False)`, `DeclaredEntity.attributes` is `dict[str, Any]`, and `broadcast` uses `json.dumps(default=str)`. The same `declared_entity_from` builds `GET /api/apps`, so any input that broke the publish would break the listing too, and that bug would be loud anyway. A cancelled job during the broadcast's lock wait (worker shutdown) also loses the delta silently, but shutdown clears every client anyway.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: a publish bug after the commit makes `set()` raise for state that is already committed, and the delta waits for the next poll.
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation: a publish bug after the commit makes `set()` raise for state that is already committed, and the delta waits for the next poll.

findings.title: Every `set()` builds and double-serializes the entity message even when no `/ws` client is connected
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: apps that `set()` many sensors at a high rate, such as the 25-sensor corpus app, with the web UI closed. `publish_entity_state` always builds `DeclaredEntity`, `EntityStateChangedData` and `model_dump()`, then `broadcast` runs `json.loads(json.dumps(...))` before it looks at the client set. All of it runs synchronously inside the single writer job. D2's table priced the cost as "one short lock and a `put_nowait` per client", which leaves out the serialization. The saving only applies to installs with neither hass-hassette nor a UI tab connected, since hass-hassette keeps a client connected whenever it runs. No measurement shows the cost matters.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: every `set()` pays the message build and serialization even with no `/ws` client connected.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: every `set()` pays the message build and serialization even with no `/ws` client connected.

findings.title: `listen()` JSON-decodes every frame to read its tag, then decodes matched frames a second time
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a large installation whose busy instances produce big `execution_completed` batches. D8 skips ignored types "without validating", and pydantic validation is indeed skipped. But `decode()` runs `json.loads` on every whole frame to read `type`, and for a matched type `parse_payload` runs `validate_json` on the same text again. The consumer runs on Home Assistant's event loop. D8's table row "`execution_completed` parse cost: None" means the pydantic cost, which compares the options fairly, but the JSON decode is still paid on every frame.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `listen` fully decodes every frame to read its type, and matched frames twice.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: `listen` fully decodes every frame to read its type, and matched frames twice.

findings.title: Two classes in `types=` with the same tag silently keep only the last one
findings.why_it_matters: `message_classes` builds a dict, so `by_tag[tags[0]] = message_class` overwrites an earlier class with the same `type` tag. A caller who passes `EntityStateChangedWsMessage` and a subclass of it gets only the later one, without being told. D8's promise ("an instance of one of the requested classes") still holds, but which class wins depends on argument order.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: two `types=` classes sharing a tag keep only the last one passed.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: two `types=` classes sharing a tag keep only the last one passed.

findings.title: A connection reset while aiohttp auto-answers a server ping escapes `listen` as a raw aiohttp exception
findings.why_it_matters: D9 promises "no raw aiohttp exception escapes" `listen`. The critic's broad claim, that reader errors on a reset escape `ws.receive()`, doesn't hold on the installed aiohttp 3.14.5: `receive()` catches `ClientError` and returns a CLOSED message, catches any other exception and returns an ERROR message, and `close()` swallows its own write errors, so those paths end as `HassetteConnectionError` through `stream_ended_error`. One path does escape. `receive()` answers a server PING with `await self.pong(...)` outside its try block, and the writer raises `ClientConnectionResetError` (a `ClientError`) when the transport is already closing. uvicorn's `websockets-sansio` backend sends keepalive pings (default every 20 s), so a reset that lands while a ping is buffered lets a raw aiohttp exception out of `listen`. A caller that catches `HassetteClientError` to reconnect would miss it, and the stream task dies until the integration reloads. The 30 s poll keeps HA's state current meanwhile.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a reset that lands while aiohttp is answering a server ping can let `aiohttp.ClientConnectionResetError` escape `listen` unmapped.
findings.chosen: A: Wrap `ws.receive()` in `listen` and `wait_for_connected` with `except aiohttp.ClientError`, mapped through `transport.failure` like a connect failure.
findings.choice_reason: Let me pick: fix 9 at least

findings.title: The `connected` frame carries no `boot_id`
findings.why_it_matters: D5's accepted limitation (sketch challenge Finding 10): a hassette restart between `connected` and the listing fetch can let old-boot deltas still queued on the old socket overwrite the new boot's listing until the reconnect refetches. A `boot_id` on `connected` would let a client spot the mismatch. The critic only notes that adding the field later is additive. That supports deferring it, not changing the stance.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `connected` carries no `boot_id`, so D5's restart window stays open until a reconnect refetches.
findings.chosen: Spell out the same-boot apply rule in the docs and on_connected docstring (apply a delta only if its boot_id equals the applied listing's); no wire change
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether boot_id on connected has a downside; chose the consumer-side same-boot rule instead

findings.title: The unwired (harness) and "service present, no clients" publish paths have no test, and the cross-layer private read is unpinned
